newsitem.title: GREECE: Angry Greek farmers play hide-and-seek with police.
newsitem.headline: Angry Greek farmers play hide-and-seek with police.

text.p: Police helicopters and riot squads played hide-and-seek on Tuesday with tractor convoys driven across open country by farmers bent on blocking highways in a mass protest.

Hundreds of tractors were turned back by police guarding key road junctions in the central Thessaly region but the farmers sneaked around the checkpoints by tracking through vast cotton fields, witnesses said.
They played cat-and-mouse with police, drawing them into fields and getting them stuck away from the checkpoints while other farmers tried to get past.
The government successfully waited out a crippling 25-day farmers' road blockade in December which virtually cut the country in two, and this time has vowed to keep roads open.
"We have every legal right to take measures to preserve normality. We want to prevent a road blockade," government spokesman Dimitris Reppas told reporters.
The government threatened to use force if necessary to thwart any new attempt to block roads. The farmers vowed to continue with their plans but announced they would not clash with police.

About 5,000 police, many in riot gear, and helicopters were dispatched to the area to prevent the farmers from taking over the roads for a second time. "Can you believe it? They sent riot squads to our little village. All we want to do is protest," a farmer driving his tractor shouted at reporters.
"Terrorism does not work on farmers. Their problems are so deep that all the helicopters and police will not hinder them," farmers' representative Vangelis Boutas said.

The farmers gave up the December blockade because of the Christmas holidays but vowed to bring their tractors back to block highways unless their demands for higher price supports, cheaper fuel and tax cuts were met.
Prime Minister Costas Simitis has turned down most of their demands, saying the state budget cannot afford to spend an extra drachma on any specific group.
He said his strict 1997 budget, described as the toughest in 15 years, along with tight new incomes and tax policies, were necessary to turn the ailing economy around.
